item.stem:
Heights of adult women in the United States are normally distributed with a mean of 64 inches and a standard deviation of 2.5 inches. A researcher takes a random sample of 100 women.

What is the sampling distribution of the sample mean x̄?

options.text: Normal with mean 64 and standard deviation 2.5
options.rationale: A student choosing this believes the sampling distribution has the same standard deviation as the population (B9), even though they correctly identify the mean as 64 (A3). They do not apply the formula SE = σ/√n.

options.text: Normal with mean 64 and standard deviation 2.5/√100
options.rationale: This is correct. The mean of the sampling distribution equals the population mean of 64 (A3), and the standard error is σ/√n = 2.5/10 = 0.25, which correctly reflects how larger sample sizes reduce variability (A7).

options.text: Normal with mean 64/√100 and standard deviation 2.5/√100
options.rationale: A student choosing this correctly reduces the standard deviation by √n (A7) but incorrectly also divides the mean by √n (B13), believing that the mean of the sampling distribution depends on sample size.

options.text: Normal with mean 64/√100 and standard deviation 2.5
options.rationale: A student choosing this holds two misconceptions: they believe the mean of the sampling distribution changes with sample size (B13) by dividing by √n, and they retain the population standard deviation unchanged (B9), not recognizing that standard error decreases with larger samples.

item.explanation: This item probes four facets through a concrete numerical scenario. The correct answer (B) requires knowing that the mean of the sampling distribution equals the population mean (A3) and that the standard error is σ/√n, reflecting how larger samples reduce spread (A7). Option A isolates the B9 misconception: the student knows the mean is correct but thinks the spread of the sampling distribution is the same as the population's SD. Option C isolates B13: the student applies the √n reduction correctly to SD but wrongly applies it to the mean as well. Option D combines both misconceptions (B9 and B13), scaling the mean by √n while leaving the SD unchanged.
